About

An aspiring researcher

I hold a B.Tech in Materials Engineering and am currently completing a two-year Master's in Materials Science and Engineering. I'm looking for a Master's thesis position that I can extend into a PhD one where I can keep working at the intersection of computational and experimental materials science.

My primary interest lies in sustainable alloy design I want to understand materials well enough, from the atomic scale up, to design them more responsibly. One of the ways I enjoy this is through characterizing the effects of impurities and defects.

I'm deliberately building fluency on both sides of that intersection, because I think the most interesting materials questions today don't yield to either approach alone.

Research

Previous Works

Copper Metallurgy — Ongoing

Impurities in Closed-Loop Processing of Copper

Studying recycled copper as it's pushed through severe plastic deformation, to understand how residual impurities affect mechanical and electrical performance.

Central question: how do impurities affect the mechanical and electrical properties of the material and what are the suitable processing conditions to minimize their impact?

IIT Gandhinagar

Annealing Temperature Effects on Pearlite

Tracked inter-lamellar spacing, hardness, and grain size of pearlitic steel across a range of annealing temperatures.

As the annealing temperature increased, inter-lamellar spacing widened and hardness decreased.

Indian Institute of Science

Beyond-Si Photovoltaics via DFT (VASP)

Investigated Na2MgSnS4, a rhombohedral, layered candidate photovoltaic material with a disordered initial structure, focusing on their various defect formation tendencies.

Found negative formation energy for the isolated Na–Mg antisite, and low formation energies for antisite clusters (NaMg + MgNa, MgSn + SnMg), making them highly undesirable for electron transport.

IIT Gandhinagar

Sustainable Synthesis of Green Carbon Dots

Explored microwave-assisted synthesis of carbon dots for metal-ion sensing, and separately synthesized carbon dots from medicinal plant and pollen from flowers.

Plant-derived carbon dots showed radical-scavenging properties and specificity towards certain metal ions making them promising candidates for developing low cost sensors.

Writing

Notes from the bench and the terminal

Research Statement

From Pearlite to Photovoltaics: Why I Want to Spend My PhD at the Intersection of Computation and Experiment

I still remember staring at EBSD and SEM images for the first time and realizing that everything I'd learned about "materials" in a textbook was really a story about atoms deciding, under pressure, where to go. That moment has quietly shaped every project I've chosen since.

Read the full post

Materials science tends to split people into two camps: the ones who run experiments and the ones who run simulations. I aspire be fluent in both. I want to be able to look at a micrograph and know what processing history produced it, and to look at a simulation and know what experimental data would validate it. I want to be able to take a material from the electron microscope to the terminal and back again, with each side correcting the other. And I want to do that with sustainability as a constraint I design into the problem rather than bolt on afterward.

Learning to see impurities as a design variable, not a defect

My current research looks at impurities in the closed-loop processing of copper. Copper that has already lived a life as some other product and is now being recycled and reshaped through severe plastic deformation. The central question is deceptively simple: how do these residual impurities evolve during the processing and affect the material's properties? But answering it well means treating impurities not as contamination to be eliminated, but as a variable to be characterized, understood, and eventually engineered around. This is a mindset I want to carry with me in my research. As we strive and steadily inch towards a circular economy, understanding what "impure" metal can and can't do isn't a tangential perspective anymore it's the focus.

Reading a microstructure like a timeline

Prior to this, at IIT Gandhinagar, I studied how annealing temperature reshapes the pearlitic microstructure of steel. The results were intuitive once I'd measured it, but quite amazing striking to actually watch unfold. It was my first real lesson in a principle I now use everywhere, that microstructure is a record of processing history, and if you learn to read it carefully enough, you can work backward from a micrograph to the choices that produced it, or forward from a set of choices to the properties you'll get.

Testing what "beyond silicon" photovoltaics could look like, one defect at a time

This project pushed me to think like a computational materials scientist first: to treat defect chemistry as the thing actually governing whether a material works.

Designing sustainability into synthesis itself

My other project at IIT Gandhinagar turned the sustainability question toward synthesis. I worked on the sustainable synthesis of green carbon dots, using microwave-assisted synthesis for metal-ion sensing applications, and separately found that carbon dots synthesized from medicinal plant sources exhibited genuine radical-scavenging properties. Both strands of this work reflect something I care about beyond any single materials system: that "sustainable" shouldn't just describe end-of-life recycling, it should describe the synthesis route itself, from the reagents we choose to the energy we spend making the material in the first place.

What I'm looking for next

A method of asking questions. I want to characterize a material experimentally, model it computationally, and let each side complement the other, with having a thorough focus on sustainability

If this aligns with the kind of work and thinking your lab values, I would be grateful for the opportunity to discuss it further.
